newsitem.title: UK: HORSE RACING-GRAND NATIONAL TO GO AHEAD TWO DAYS LATE.
newsitem.headline: HORSE RACING-GRAND NATIONAL TO GO AHEAD TWO DAYS LATE.

text.p: The Grand National steeplechase, called off because of bomb threats on Saturday, will go ahead on Monday, organisers said on Sunday.

Aintree racecourse managing director Charles Barnett said the race, the 150th Grand National, had been rescheduled for 1600 GMT on Monday after consultations with trainers, owners and other interested parties.
Barnett told a news conference: "Trainers have been notified and the vast majority of those contacted have already indicated that their horses will take part in the rescheduled running of the race."
Thirty-eight runners were lined up on Saturday but the race was abandoned after two coded bomb warnings.
A crowd of 70,000 were evacuated from the racecourse and three controlled explosions were carried out on packages later deemed to be harmless.
Thousands of people, forbidden by police to collect their cars from the racecourse, spent the night on the floors of local sports halls and schools.
Aintree chairman Lord Daresbury said: "The nation shared in Saturday's disappointment but we all feel there is a huge collective will for the Grand National to go ahead."
Barnett said: "Working closely with the police we are going to great lengths to ensure that we stage the big race on Monday. Our staff are sparing no effort in preparing the course and facilities.
"We are overwhelmed by the support and encouragement we have received from so many quarters and believe it right for the race to be rescheduled."
No vehicles will be allowed on the racecourse on Monday. Barnett said extra public transport was being laid on.
Paul Stephenson, the local assistant chief constable and director of operations, said no bombs had been found at Aintree.
"Nobody has claimed responsibility and we can all draw our conclusions," he said, adding that police supported the decision to run the race on Monday.
The scenes at Aintree followed massive disruption on motorways in central England last week after the discovery of two Irish Republican Army (IRA) bombs on road bridges.

Barnett said he was confident the race could go ahead on Monday. "I am assured we can get the course right in time although substantial damage has been done to the running rail and some of the fences," he said.
